paragraphs: “You don’t know how much you encourage us, Dmitri Fyodorovitch, by being so ready to answer,” said Nikolay Parfenovitch, looking animated, with obvious satisfaction shining in his very prominent, short-sighted, light gray eyes, from which he had just taken off his spectacles. “And you made a very fair point about mutual trust. Without it, it is sometimes simply impossible to get anywhere in cases this important, if the suspect really hopes and wants to defend himself and is in a position to do so. We, for our part, will do everything in our power, and you can see for yourself how we are conducting the case. Do you approve, Ippolit Kirillovitch?” He turned to the prosecutor.
“Oh, certainly,” replied the prosecutor. His tone was rather cold next to Nikolay Parfenovitch’s eagerness.

I should say once and for all that Nikolay Parfenovitch, who had only recently come to our town, had felt a marked respect for Ippolit Kirillovitch, our prosecutor, from the very first, and had become almost his bosom friend. He was nearly the only person who believed without reservation in Ippolit Kirillovitch’s extraordinary talents as a psychologist and an orator, and in the justice of his grievance. He had heard of him in Petersburg. And in return, young Nikolay Parfenovitch was the only person in the whole world whom our “unappreciated” prosecutor genuinely liked. On the way to Mokroe they had found time to agree on how to handle the present case. Now, as they sat at the table, the sharp-witted junior caught and interpreted every sign on his senior colleague’s face—half a word, a glance, a wink.
“Gentlemen, just let me tell my story my own way and don’t interrupt me with petty questions, and I’ll tell you everything in a moment,” said Mitya excitedly.

“Excellent! Thank you. But before we go on to hear your account, will you let me ask about one more small fact that interests us greatly? I mean the ten roubles you borrowed yesterday at about five o’clock, against the security of your pistols, from your friend Pyotr Ilyitch Perhotin.”
“I pawned them, gentlemen. I pawned them for ten roubles. What more is there? That’s all there is to it. As soon as I got back to town, I pawned them.”
“You got back to town? So you had been out of town?”
“Yes, I made a trip of forty versts into the country. Didn’t you know?”
The prosecutor and Nikolay Parfenovitch exchanged glances.

“Well, how would it be if you began your story with an orderly account of everything you did yesterday, from the morning on? Let us ask, for instance, why you were away from the town, and exactly when you left and when you came back—all those facts.”

“You should have asked me like that from the beginning,” cried Mitya, laughing aloud, “and, if you like, we won’t start from yesterday but from the morning of the day before. Then you’ll understand how, why and where I went. The day before yesterday, gentlemen, I went to a merchant in the town named Samsonov, to borrow three thousand roubles from him on safe security. It was a pressing matter, gentlemen. I suddenly needed it badly.”
“Allow me to interrupt you,” the prosecutor put in politely. “Why did you need just that sum, three thousand, so urgently?”

“Oh, gentlemen, you needn’t go into details, how, when and why, and why just so much money and not so much, and all that rigmarole. Why, it would run to three volumes, and then you’d want an epilogue!”
Mitya said all this with the good-natured but impatient familiarity of a man who is eager to tell the whole truth and is full of the best intentions.

“Gentlemen!”—he corrected himself hurriedly—“don’t be annoyed with me for being so restless, I ask you again. Believe me, I feel the greatest respect for you and I understand the real state of affairs. Don’t think I’m drunk. I’m quite sober now. And anyway, being drunk wouldn’t get in the way. With me, you know, it’s like the saying: ‘When he is sober, he is a fool; when he is drunk, he is a wise man.’ Ha ha! But I see, gentlemen, that it isn’t proper to joke with you, not until we’ve had our explanation, I mean. And I have my own dignity to keep up, too. I understand the difference for the moment perfectly well. After all, I’m in the position of a criminal, so I’m far from being on equal terms with you. And it’s your job to watch me. I can’t expect you to pat me on the head for what I did to Grigory, because you can’t break old men’s heads for nothing. I suppose you’ll put me away for him for six months, or maybe a year, in a house of correction. I don’t know what the punishment is—but it will be without loss of the rights of my rank, without loss of my rank, won’t it? So you see, gentlemen, I understand the distinction between us.... But you must see that you could baffle God Himself with such questions. ‘How did you step? Where did you step? When did you step? And on what did you step?’ I’ll get mixed up if you keep on like this, and you’ll write it all down against me. And where will that lead? To nothing! And even if I’m talking nonsense now, let me finish, and you, gentlemen, being men of honor and refinement, will forgive me! I’ll finish by asking you, gentlemen, to drop that conventional way of questioning. I mean, starting from some miserable trifle, how I got up, what I had for breakfast, how I spat, and where I spat, and so distracting the criminal’s attention, and then suddenly stunning him with an overwhelming question: ‘Whom did you murder? Whom did you rob?’ Ha ha! That’s your standard method, that’s where all your cunning comes in. You can catch peasants off guard like that, but not me. I know the tricks. I’ve been in the service, too. Ha ha ha! You’re not angry, gentlemen? You forgive my impertinence?” he cried, looking at them with a good nature that was almost startling. “It’s only Mitya Karamazov, you know, so you can overlook it. It would be inexcusable in a sensible man, but you can forgive it in Mitya. Ha ha!”

Nikolay Parfenovitch listened, and laughed too. The prosecutor did not laugh, but he kept his eyes fixed keenly on Mitya, as though afraid to miss the least syllable, the slightest movement, the smallest twitch of any feature of his face.

“That’s how we have treated you from the beginning,” said Nikolay Parfenovitch, still laughing. “We haven’t tried to throw you off by asking how you got up in the morning and what you had for breakfast. In fact, we began with questions of the greatest importance.”

“I understand. I saw it and I appreciated it, and I appreciate even more your present kindness to me, an unheard-of kindness, worthy of your noble hearts. We three here are gentlemen, so let everything be on a footing of mutual trust between educated, well-bred people, who share the common bond of noble birth and honor. In any case, let me look on you as my best friends at this moment of my life, at this moment when my honor is under attack. That’s no insult to you, gentlemen, is it?”
“On the contrary. You’ve put all that so well, Dmitri Fyodorovitch,” Nikolay Parfenovitch answered with dignified approval.
“And enough of those petty questions, gentlemen, all those tricky questions!” cried Mitya enthusiastically. “Or there’s simply no knowing where we’ll end up! Is there?”

“I will follow your sensible advice completely,” the prosecutor interposed, addressing Mitya. “I don’t withdraw my question, however. It is now vitally important for us to know exactly why you needed that sum, I mean precisely three thousand.”
“Why I needed it?... Oh, for one thing and another.... Well, it was to pay a debt.”
“A debt to whom?”

“That I absolutely refuse to answer, gentlemen. Not because I can’t, or because I wouldn’t dare, or because it would do me harm, for it’s all a paltry matter and completely trivial, but—I won’t, because it’s a matter of principle: that’s my private life, and I won’t allow any intrusion into my private life. That’s my principle. Your question has no bearing on the case, and whatever has nothing to do with the case is my private affair. I wanted to pay a debt. I wanted to pay a debt of honor, but to whom, I won’t say.”
“Allow me to make a note of that,” said the prosecutor.
“By all means. Write down that I won’t say, that I won’t. Write that I’d think it dishonorable to say. Ech! You can write it; you’ve got nothing else to do with your time.”

“Let me warn you, sir, and remind you once more, if you are unaware of it,” the prosecutor began, with a peculiar and stern impressiveness, “that you have a perfect right not to answer the questions put to you now, and we on our side have no right to extort an answer from you, if you decline to give it for one reason or another. That is entirely for you to decide. But it is our duty, on the other hand, in cases like the present one, to explain to you and set before you how much harm you will be doing yourself by refusing to give this or that piece of evidence. After that, I will ask you to continue.”
“Gentlemen, I’m not angry ... I ...” Mitya muttered, rather disconcerted. “Well, gentlemen, you see, that Samsonov I went to then ...”

We will not, of course, repeat his account of what the reader already knows. Mitya was impatiently anxious not to leave out the slightest detail. At the same time, he was in a hurry to get it over with. But as he gave his evidence it was written down, and so they had constantly to pull him up. Mitya disliked this, but put up with it; he got angry, though still good-humoredly. He did, it is true, exclaim from time to time, “Gentlemen, that’s enough to make an angel lose patience!” Or, “Gentlemen, it’s no good irritating me.”

But even though he exclaimed, he kept his genial, expansive mood for a time. So he told them how Samsonov had made a fool of him two days before. (He had fully realized by now that he had been fooled.) The sale of his watch for six roubles to get money for the journey was something new to the lawyers. They were at once very interested, and even, to Mitya’s intense indignation, thought it necessary to write the fact down as secondary confirmation that he had hardly a farthing in his pocket at the time. Little by little Mitya began to turn surly. Then, after describing his journey to see Lyagavy, the night spent in the stifling hut, and so on, he came to his return to the town. Here he began, without being particularly urged, to give a detailed account of the agonies of jealousy he had suffered over Grushenka.

He was heard with silent attention. They asked particularly about his having a place of ambush in Marya Kondratyevna’s house at the back of Fyodor Pavlovitch’s garden, from which to keep watch on Grushenka, and about Smerdyakov’s bringing him information. They laid special stress on this, and noted it down. He spoke warmly and at length of his jealousy, and though inwardly ashamed to expose his most intimate feelings to “public ignominy,” so to speak, he evidently overcame his shame in order to tell the truth. The frigid severity with which the investigating lawyer, and still more the prosecutor, stared intently at him as he told his story finally disconcerted him quite a lot.

“That boy, Nikolay Parfenovitch, to whom I was talking nonsense about women only a few days ago, and that sickly prosecutor are not worth my telling this to,” he reflected mournfully. “It’s ignominious. ‘Be patient, humble, hold thy peace.’” He ended his reflections with that line. But he pulled himself together and went on again. When he came to telling about his visit to Madame Hohlakov, his spirits revived, and he even wanted to tell a little anecdote about that lady which had nothing to do with the case. But the investigating lawyer stopped him, and civilly suggested that he move on to “more essential matters.” At last he described his despair, and told them how, when he left Madame Hohlakov’s, he thought that he’d “get three thousand if he had to murder somebody to do it.” They stopped him again and noted down that he had “meant to murder somebody.” Mitya let them write it without protest. Finally he reached the point in his story where he learned that Grushenka had deceived him and had come back from Samsonov’s as soon as he left her there, though she had said she would stay there till midnight.

“If I didn’t kill Fenya then, gentlemen, it was only because I didn’t have time,” broke from him suddenly at that point in his story. That, too, was carefully written down. Mitya waited gloomily, and was starting to tell how he ran into his father’s garden when the investigating lawyer suddenly stopped him. He opened the big portfolio that lay on the sofa beside him and took out the brass pestle.
“Do you recognize this object?” he asked, showing it to Mitya.
“Oh, yes,” he laughed gloomily. “Of course I recognize it. Let me have a look at it.... Damn it, never mind!”
“You forgot to mention it,” observed the investigating lawyer.
“Hang it all, I wouldn’t have hidden it from you. Do you think I could have managed without it? It just slipped my memory.”
“Be so good as to tell us exactly how you came to arm yourself with it.”
“Certainly, I’ll be so good, gentlemen.”
And Mitya described how he took the pestle and ran.
“But what was your purpose in arming yourself with such a weapon?”
“What purpose? No purpose. I just picked it up and ran off.”
“What for, if you had no purpose?”

Mitya’s wrath flared up. He looked intently at “the boy” and smiled gloomily and spitefully. He felt more and more ashamed that he had told “such people” the story of his jealousy so sincerely and so openly.
“Bother the pestle!” broke from him suddenly.
“But still—”
“Oh, to keep off dogs.... Oh, because it was dark.... In case anything came up.”
“But have you ever before taken a weapon with you when you went out, since you’re afraid of the dark?”
“Ugh! Damn it all, gentlemen! There’s simply no talking to you!” cried Mitya, exasperated beyond endurance, and turning to the secretary, crimson with anger, he said quickly, with fury in his voice:

“Write down at once ... at once ... ‘that I snatched up the pestle to go and kill my father ... Fyodor Pavlovitch ... by hitting him on the head with it!’ Well, are you satisfied now, gentlemen? Are your minds relieved?” he said, glaring defiantly at the lawyers.

“We quite understand that you made that statement just now out of exasperation with us and with the questions we put to you, which you consider trivial, though they are, in fact, essential,” the prosecutor remarked dryly in reply.

“Well, really, gentlemen! Yes, I took the pestle.... What does one pick things up for at such moments? I don’t know what for. I snatched it up and ran—that’s all. Because for me, gentlemen, _passons_, or I swear I won’t tell you any more.”

He sat with his elbows on the table and his head in his hand. He sat sideways to them and gazed at the wall, fighting a feeling of nausea. He had, in fact, an awful urge to get up and declare that he wouldn’t say another word, “not if you hang me for it.”

“You see, gentlemen,” he said at last, with difficulty controlling himself, “you see. I listen to you and I’m haunted by a dream.... It’s a dream I have sometimes, you know.... I often dream it—it’s always the same ... that someone is hunting me, someone I’m awfully afraid of ... that he’s hunting me in the dark, in the night ... tracking me, and I hide somewhere from him, behind a door or a cupboard, hide in a degrading way, and the worst of it is, he always knows where I am, but he pretends not to know where I am on purpose, to prolong my agony, to enjoy my terror.... That’s just what you’re doing now. It’s just like that!”
“Is that the sort of thing you dream about?” asked the prosecutor.
“Yes, it is. Don’t you want to write it down?” said Mitya, with a twisted smile.
“No; no need to write it down. But you do have strange dreams.”
“It’s not a question of dreams now, gentlemen—this is realism, this is real life! I’m a wolf and you’re the hunters. Well, hunt him down!”
“You are wrong to make such comparisons ...” began Nikolay Parfenovitch, with extraordinary softness.

“No, I’m not wrong, not at all!” Mitya flared up again, though his outburst of anger had obviously eased his heart. He grew more good-humored with every word. “You may not trust a criminal, or a man on trial tortured by your questions, but an honorable man, the honorable impulses of the heart (I say that boldly!)—no! That you must believe, you have no right indeed ... but—
Be silent, heart, Be patient, humble, hold thy peace.
Well, shall I go on?” he broke off gloomily.
“If you’ll be so kind,” answered Nikolay Parfenovitch.
